# Basic Spanish — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/spanish-basics.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/spanish-basics.ttl`](../decks/spanish-basics.ttl) · **Cards:** 120 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

120 basic Spanish words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and common phrases, and everyday nouns and verbs. The front shows the Spanish word, nouns with their article (el libro), except the days and months, whose gender is in a note; the back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number. Words, genders and meanings from Wikidata's lexemes and the US Foreign Service Institute's Spanish Basic Course (public domain), checked against the Real Academia Española's dictionary, Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from two sources whose terms allow any reuse: Wikidata's lexemes and items (CC0 1.0: Spanish lemmas, genders, glosses, translations and English and Swedish labels) and the Foreign Service Institute's Spanish Basic Course (1961), a work of the United States Government with no copyright protection under 17 U.S.C. § 105 (the Spanish phrases with their meaning, and the meaning of querer and ver). The selection of words is the authors' own. The English and Swedish renderings not taken from Wikidata are the usual equivalents chosen by the authors; several of them (the English of five phrases, the Swedish of the phrases, por favor and abuelo/abuela) are the same short stock glosses that English Wiktionary or Folkets lexikon give, as the method says. Single words and fixed greetings such as "see you later" or "god morgon" are facts of usage, not protectable expression, so this does not carry their licences into the deck; no definition, example, comment or list was taken from them. The Real Academia Española's dictionary (all rights reserved), English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0), Swedish Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Folkets lexikon (CC BY-SA 2.5) were used for verification only. So no source requires attribution or share-alike for the deck, although all are credited in its provenance. The quotations in this provenance report are not covered by the deck's CC0 dedication or the repository's MIT licence: quotations from the RAE dictionary (© Real Academia Española, all rights reserved) are short citations for verification, cut to what the check needs; quotations from English and Swedish Wiktionary are © Wiktionary contributors, CC BY-SA 4.0; quotations from Folkets lexikon are CC BY-SA 2.5; quotations from the FSI course are in the public domain.

## Method

1. The research, drafting and cross-checking of this deck were done by AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks against Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators, followed by six independent AI review rounds (quality control below). The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert (a teacher of Spanish or a translator).
2. Word list. A candidate list of 120 words for a first Spanish course was drawn up by hand from the brief's categories (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and phrases; everyday nouns; everyday verbs), choosing the most basic word for each concept and avoiding words whose everyday form differs between Spain and Latin America. No frequency list or textbook word list was copied.
3. Wikidata lexemes. The SPARQL query 1 fetched every Spanish lexeme (language Q1321) whose lemma is a candidate, with its category, gender (P5185), senses, glosses and sense items (P5137). Lemmas not found, or found without senses, were looked up with the lexeme search (API calls 2). The full JSON of the lexeme chosen for each word (the noun lexeme for nouns, the verb lexeme for verbs, and so on) was fetched with API calls 3, and the English and Swedish lexemes named by the senses' translation statements (P5972) with API calls 4. Feminine family words (hermana, hija, abuela) are forms of the lexemes hermano, hijo and abuelo, whose forms carry the feminine and singular features.
4. Wikidata items. The items linked from the senses (P5137) were fetched with API calls 5 and gave English and Swedish labels for days, months, colours, numbers and everyday things. For concepts with no item link (colours yellow, white, green and grey; brother, sister, woman, man, street, window, hand, work; greetings) items were found with the item search (API calls 6) and fetched with API calls 7.
5. Phrases. Wikidata has no Spanish lexeme for buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches, gracias, de nada, lo siento, hasta luego or mucho gusto. Their Spanish form and meaning were taken from the basic sentences of Units 1 and 2 of the Foreign Service Institute's Spanish Basic Course (1961, a US Government work in the public domain), read in the Internet Archive's OCR text (calls 10 and 11) and compared with the scanned layout of the English and Spanish columns. The English on the cards is our own choice of the usual English equivalent of that meaning, not always FSI's wording: FSI has "So long" (card: see you later), "Glad to meet you" (nice to meet you), "thanks" (thank you), "Good evening" (good evening, good night, the second added from RAE's "al irse a acostar") and "I'm very sorry" for Lo siento mucho (I'm sorry). These English backs are also the first glosses in English Wiktionary, which was consulted (step 8); they are short stock phrases, not protectable expression.
6. Writing the cards. The front is the Spanish word as in the lexeme's lemma (or form), nouns preceded by the definite article that matches their gender (el agua takes el although feminine). The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits (untagged, since digits have no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists; otherwise they are the standard Swedish equivalent, chosen by the authors and checked in Folkets lexikon (step 8). For the greetings and phrases, por favor and abuelo/abuela, where no CC0 source gives Swedish, the Swedish on the card is the same as the Folkets entry it was checked against (for example good morning → god morgon, pleased to meet you → trevligt att träffas, grandfather → farfar, morfar); these are single words or fixed greetings, facts of usage rather than protectable expression, and no Folkets definitions, examples or selection were used. Swedish uses lower case for days and months. Where one English word maps to two Swedish words (ir: gå or åka; vivir: leva or bo; abuelo: farfar or morfar) both are given.
7. Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and is confirmed by the dictionary: irregular genders (el agua, la mano, el día), the gender of every day and month, the short form un, cien as the short form of ciento used for 100 by itself and before a noun, mil or millones (101–199 use ciento), the plural padres (parents), mujer also meaning wife, querer also meaning to love, sí versus si, ser versus estar (with ser for where an event takes place), naranja the colour versus la naranja the fruit (with a front note "colour"), noche also covering the evening after dark (buenas noches), lo siento also used in sympathy, Swedish requests often ending with tack rather than a word for please, the Swedish gå/åka distinction, buenos días being said until midday or lunch, and buenas tardes being used until nightfall. Notes are our own wording.
8. Cross-checking. Every Spanish word was looked up in the Real Academia Española's Diccionario de la lengua española (calls 12): its spelling, its grammatical gender against the article on the card, and its first relevant definition (quoted in each card's evidence). Every English meaning was checked against the Spanish section of the English Wiktionary (calls 13). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (calls 14), English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match. Where the FSI vocabulary appendix lists the word, its English gloss was compared as well. A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quote is what the source returned (the look-up logic is recorded with calls 11–14); the raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published. Quotations from the RAE dictionary are cut to the headword, the grammatical label and the first words of the sense, marked with "…".
9. Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (the Spanish, English and Swedish label or alias of each linked item that matches the card's text, and the multilingual digit label of each number) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026.
10. Excluded: words whose usual form differs by region (car: coche/carro/auto; brown: marrón/café; juice: zumo/jugo; computer: ordenador/computadora), saber/conocer (both "to know", which needs more context than a flashcard gives), niño (child or boy), the morning/tomorrow pair mañana, and tiempo (time or weather), since each would need more than one answer.
11. Review rounds. Three independent AI reviewers (factual accuracy; language and translation; licensing and documentation) checked the deck, followed by two final re-check reviewers who re-checked the changed cards, every third card, the metadata and the documentation, and a final full-deck reviewer. Their findings were verified against the sources before any change: the Folkets entries sorry, ledsen, beklaga and wife, the RAE entries ser (acepción 7), día, mañana, tarde and anochecer, the FSI basic sentences for querer and ver (calls 15–17), and the Swedish Wiktionary entries buenos días, buenas tardes and naranja (call 18); in the re-checks, the mul labels of the number items (call 19), the English Wiktionary usage notes of cien (call 20) and the sense items of the lexemes hijo and abuelo (call 21). The resulting changes are listed under quality control, rounds 1–6.

## Selection

120 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, orange); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and common phrases; 25 everyday nouns (house, water, bread, milk, apple, book, table, chair, door, window, dog, cat, city, street, school, man, woman, friend, money, work, hand, day, night, year, week); and 19 common verbs in the infinitive (ser, estar, tener, hacer, ir, venir, hablar, comer, beber, vivir, querer, poder, ver, decir, escribir, leer, dormir, trabajar, comprar). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list or textbook. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except the eight phrases noted in the method, which come from the public-domain FSI course. Left out: words whose everyday form differs between Spain and Latin America (coche/carro, marrón/café, zumo/jugo, ordenador/computadora), word pairs a beginner cannot tell apart on a single card without context (saber/conocer), words with two equally common meanings (mañana, tiempo, niño), and brown and purple (several competing words). Colours are given in the masculine singular; the feminine form is in a note. Days and months are given without an article, as they are usually written; their gender is in a note on every day and month card.

## Queries

**1. Spanish lexemes (Q1321) for every candidate lemma, with lexical category, grammatical gender (P5185), senses, English and Swedish glosses and the item for each sense (P5137). POST to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql** (Wikidata (Spanish lexemes and items))

```
SELECT ?lexeme ?lemma ?category ?gender ?sense ?glossEn ?glossSv ?item WHERE {
  VALUES ?lemma { "cero"@es "uno"@es "dos"@es "tres"@es "cuatro"@es "cinco"@es "seis"@es "siete"@es "ocho"@es "nueve"@es "diez"@es "once"@es "doce"@es "trece"@es "catorce"@es "quince"@es "dieciséis"@es "diecisiete"@es "dieciocho"@es "diecinueve"@es "veinte"@es "treinta"@es "cuarenta"@es "cincuenta"@es "sesenta"@es "setenta"@es "ochenta"@es "noventa"@es "cien"@es "lunes"@es "martes"@es "miércoles"@es "jueves"@es "viernes"@es "sábado"@es "domingo"@es "enero"@es "febrero"@es "marzo"@es "abril"@es "mayo"@es "junio"@es "julio"@es "agosto"@es "septiembre"@es "octubre"@es "noviembre"@es "diciembre"@es "rojo"@es "azul"@es "verde"@es "amarillo"@es "negro"@es "blanco"@es "gris"@es "naranja"@es "madre"@es "padre"@es "hermano"@es "hermana"@es "hijo"@es "hija"@es "abuelo"@es "abuela"@es "hola"@es "adiós"@es "buenos días"@es "buenas tardes"@es "buenas noches"@es "gracias"@es "por favor"@es "de nada"@es "sí"@es "lo siento"@es "hasta luego"@es "mucho gusto"@es "casa"@es "agua"@es "pan"@es "leche"@es "manzana"@es "libro"@es "mesa"@es "silla"@es "puerta"@es "ventana"@es "perro"@es "gato"@es "ciudad"@es "calle"@es "escuela"@es "hombre"@es "mujer"@es "amigo"@es "dinero"@es "trabajo"@es "mano"@es "día"@es "noche"@es "año"@es "semana"@es "ser"@es "estar"@es "tener"@es "hacer"@es "ir"@es "venir"@es "hablar"@es "comer"@es "beber"@es "vivir"@es "querer"@es "poder"@es "ver"@es "decir"@es "escribir"@es "leer"@es "dormir"@es "trabajar"@es "comprar"@es }
  ?lexeme dct:language wd:Q1321 ;
          wikibase:lemma ?lemma ;
          wikibase:lexicalCategory ?category .
  OPTIONAL { ?lexeme wdt:P5185 ?gender . }
  OPTIONAL {
    ?lexeme ontolex:sense ?sense .
    OPTIONAL { ?sense skos:definition ?glossEn . FILTER(LANG(?glossEn) = "en") }
    OPTIONAL { ?sense skos:definition ?glossSv . FILTER(LANG(?glossSv) = "sv") }
    OPTIONAL { ?sense wdt:P5137 ?item . }
  }
}
ORDER BY ?lemma ?lexeme ?sense
```

# text extraction (Python):
class P(HTMLParser):  # collects the text inside the element with id="resultados", skipping <script> and <style>
    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if dict(attrs).get("id") == "resultados": self.on = True
        if tag in ("script", "style"): self.skip += 1
    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in ("script", "style") and self.skip: self.skip -= 1
    def handle_data(self, data):
        if self.on and not self.skip: self.parts.append(data)
t = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "".join(p.parts)).strip().split("Palabra del día")[0]

**14. Folkets lexikon, both directions, and its about page (licence); entries looked up by headword ("|" compound marks removed) and by idiom; the matching code is given after the URLs** (Folkets lexikon (English–Swedish and Swedish–English))

```
https://folkets-lexikon.csc.kth.se/folkets/folkets_en_sv_public.xml
https://folkets-lexikon.csc.kth.se/folkets/folkets_sv_en_public.xml
https://folkets-lexikon.csc.kth.se/folkets/om.html
# index and matching (Python):
for w in ET.parse(fn).getroot().iter("word"):
    head = w.get("value").replace("|", "")
    tr = [t.get("value") for t in w.findall("translation")]
    idx.setdefault(head.lower(), []).append(("word", head, w.get("class"), tr))
    for idm in w.findall("idiom"):
        itr = [t.get("value") for t in idm.findall("translation")]
        idx.setdefault(idm.get("value").lower().rstrip("!.").strip(), []).append(("idiom", head, None, itr))
# a card's word matches when some entry of idx[word.lower()] (entries of the card's word class first) has a translation
# equal, ignoring case and a final "!" or ".", to the card's text in the other language
```

## Quality control

7 rounds, 43 findings: 34 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 8 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (245 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 120 cards: every Spanish form, gender, English and Swedish meaning and note against the content sources and the three verification sources; the builder's Wikidata checks.

Every card has evidence from a content source (Wikidata or the FSI course) and at least two of the verification sources; RAE, Wiktionary and Folkets agree with every card as written. The genders on the cards (article el or la) match the RAE entries for all 33 nouns and the Wikidata lexemes wherever the lexeme records a gender. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the Spanish, English and Swedish labels or aliases of 93 linked items (245 checks) and the digit label of every number; they all pass. Discrepancies between sources and how they were resolved are listed below.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| dia | Wikidata's Swedish label for day (Q573) is "dygn" (a 24-hour period), not "dag". | Kept "dag", the everyday word covering both senses of día, confirmed by Folkets lexikon (day → dag). The Swedish label check for Q573 was not added. | no change needed |
| abuelo, abuela | Wikidata's Swedish labels for grandfather and grandmother (Q9238344, Q9235758) are the descriptive "förälders far" and "förälders mor"; Swedish has no single neutral word. | The cards give "farfar eller morfar" and "farmor eller mormor", as Folkets lexikon translates grandfather and grandmother. No Swedish label check for these items. | no change needed |
| cuarenta | Wikidata lexeme L565768 (cuarenta) has grammatical gender feminine, while the other number lexemes are masculine and the RAE treats numbers used as nouns as masculine. | The number cards show no article, so the card is unaffected; the discrepancy is recorded here for Wikidata's editors. | no change needed |
| amigo, noche | The Wikidata lexemes for amigo (L230374) and noche (L57895) record no grammatical gender. | The article comes from the RAE entries ("amigo, ga", noche "f.") and, for noche, from FSI's feminine "Buenas noches"; both are facts, not copied text. | no change needed |
| hombre | The item for man (Q8441) has the Spanish label "varón"; "hombre" is an alias. | The check uses the alias; RAE acepción 3 ("Varón que ha llegado a la edad adulta") and Wiktionary ("man (adult male human)") confirm the meaning. | no change needed |
| buenas-noches | FSI renders Buenas noches as "Good evening"; Wiktionary gives both good evening and good night; RAE says it is used "durante la noche o al irse a acostar". | The back gives both: good evening, good night / god kväll, god natt. | fixed |
| buenas-tardes | Wiktionary also gives "good evening" for buenas tardes. | Kept good afternoon (FSI, Wikidata Q19279334) and added a note that la tarde runs from midday until nightfall (RAE tarde, acepción 1). | fixed |
| por-favor | Swedish has no exact equivalent of please; Folkets lexikon lists varsågod, tack, ja tack, snälla. | The back gives snälla, with a note that Swedish requests usually end with tack. | fixed |
| septiembre, amarillo | Folkets lexikon's English–Swedish entry for September has the misspelt translation "septembere", and its entries for yellow give only derived senses (gulna, feg). | Checked in the Swedish–English direction instead (september → September, gul → yellow). | no change needed |
| ser, estar | Both verbs are "to be" / "att vara", so the backs are not unique. | Each has a note on when it is used. The deck is studied front to back only, so a back never has to identify one of the two. | fixed |
| trabajo | The item first found for work, Q6958747, is a redirect to Q268378, so the builder's label checks against Q6958747 failed (the query service has no labels on a redirect). | The checks and evidence use Q268378 (es "trabajo", en "work", sv "arbete"). | fixed |
| — | The FSI course teaches Latin American Spanish. | Only words and phrases that are standard everywhere were kept; each is in the RAE dictionary without a regional mark in the sense used. | no change needed |
| — | The builder's checks cannot verify lexeme statements (gender, forms, senses). | These were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026 (queries 1 and 3) and compared with the RAE entries by script; all genders agree. | no change needed |

### Round 1: Factual accuracy (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent factual accuracy reviewer · **Scope:** All 120 cards, re-checked mainly against Swedish Wiktionary's Spanish entries, the RAE entries and the FSI scan; the builder's Wikidata checks re-run.

No factual errors found; all numbers, days, months, colours, family words, nouns (with genders), phrases and verbs confirmed, and the Wikidata checks pass. Two warnings (the Swedish back of lo siento covered only the apology; the day and month cards after lunes and enero gave no gender) and three suggestions (buenos días until midday, ser for the location of events, naranja colour versus fruit). All five were verified and fixed.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| lo-siento | The Swedish back "förlåt" covers only the apology sense of lo siento, not regret or sympathy (lo siento mucho on hearing of a death). | Verified: FSI glosses lo siento as "it (I) regret", RAE sentir 5 "Lamentar … Sentir la muerte de un amigo", Folkets förlåt is "fras för att be om ursäkt" while sorry (jj) → ledsen with the sympathy explanation. The Swedish back is now "jag är ledsen, förlåt", the note adds that it is also said in sympathy, and the Folkets entries sorry, ledsen and beklaga are in the evidence. | fixed |
| martes … domingo, febrero … diciembre | The description promises nouns with their article, but days and months have none and only lunes and enero say they are masculine. | Verified: RAE marks every day and month "m." and the Wikidata lexemes give masculine. Every day card now has the note "Days of the week are masculine (el martes) …" and every month card the month note; the description and selection say that days and months carry their gender in a note instead of an article. | fixed |
| buenos-dias | "god morgon" alone understates how long buenos días is used. | Verified: RAE "dar los buenos días: Saludar por la mañana" and mañana 1 "entre el amanecer y el mediodía, o la hora de comer o almorzar"; Swedish Wiktionary gives god morgon, god dag. Kept the back "god morgon" ("god dag" is formal or dated in Swedish) and added the note "Said all morning, until midday or lunchtime". | fixed |
| estar, ser | "Estar: where someone or something is" over-generalises; the place where an event takes place is said with ser. | Verified in RAE ser acepción 7 ("Suceder, acontecer, tener lugar. ¿Dónde fue la boda?"). The estar note now says "where someone or something is located"; the ser note adds "Also where an event takes place: la fiesta es en casa", with the RAE evidence. | fixed |
| naranja | The bare front naranja is also the noun la naranja (the fruit, apelsin), a plausible wrong answer. | Verified in RAE (naranja 1 f. fruit, 4 adj. colour) and Swedish Wiktionary. Added the front note "colour" / "färg" and a back note that the noun la naranja is the fruit. | fixed |

### Round 2: Language and translation (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent language and translation reviewer · **Scope:** All 120 cards in every language: Spanish fronts, English and Swedish backs and notes, language tags, title, description and keywords.

No errors. Two warnings (lo siento's Swedish back; the Swedish buenas tardes note said "until evening" where the English and RAE say nightfall) and five suggestions (fru in the mujer note, snälla for por favor, a note on buenos días, typographic quotes, a confusing sentence in the selection). Six were applied; the por favor suggestion was declined.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| lo-siento | "förlåt" is perdón; lo siento also expresses regret and sympathy, which needs "jag är ledsen". | Same as round 1: the Swedish back is now "jag är ledsen, förlåt" with a note on the sympathy use; the Folkets sorry → ledsen entry is in the evidence. | fixed |
| buenas-tardes | The Swedish note "tills det blir kväll" contradicts the English "until nightfall" and RAE's "anochecer". | Verified: RAE tarde 1 "entre el mediodía y el anochecer", anochecer 1 "Empezar a faltar la luz del día"; Swedish Wiktionary gives god eftermiddag, god kväll. Both notes now say "until nightfall (la tarde), so also in the early evening" / "tills det blir mörkt …, alltså även tidig kväll". | fixed |
| mujer | The Swedish note gives only the formal "hustru"; the everyday word is "fru". | Verified: Folkets wife → fru, hustru. The note is now "Även ”fru, hustru”.", with the Folkets entry in the evidence. | fixed |
| por-favor | "snälla" is a pleading, informal word; the back alone suggests it is the neutral equivalent. | Declined: "vänligen" is written and formal, not what a Swede says in speech, and Swedish has no neutral one-word equivalent. The back note already says that Swedish requests usually end with tack (en kaffe, tack), which covers the neutral case. | rejected |
| buenos-dias | God morgon is used early in the day; buenos días is said until midday or lunch. | Same as round 1: added the note "Said all morning, until midday or lunchtime (la mañana)", supported by RAE mañana acepción 1. | fixed |
| padre, mujer, si, lo-siento, querer, de-nada | Straight ASCII quotes and apostrophes in notes and backs; other library decks use typographic quotes. | Card text now uses ’ in you’re and I’m, “…” for English glosses and ”…” for Swedish glosses, as in the constellations deck. Evidence quotations keep the sources' own characters. | fixed |
| — | The selection text lists "colours given only in the masculine singular" among the exclusions. | Rewritten: "Colours are given in the masculine singular; the feminine form is in a note." as its own sentence. | fixed |

### Round 3: Licensing, attribution and documentation (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent licensing, attribution and documentation reviewer · **Scope:** Every source's licence and terms page; the method, queries and licensing text; 46 cards in detail against their evidence; the builder's Wikidata checks.

Every source's licence is recorded correctly and CC0 is defensible, but the record misdescribed where some English and Swedish wording came from, quoted the RAE dictionary at length, and claimed unpublished working files. One error, four warnings and two suggestions; all were verified and fixed.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| hasta-luego, mucho-gusto, gracias, buenas-noches, lo-siento | The method and fsi.usedFor said the phrases' English was taken from FSI, but for these five it is English Wiktionary's first gloss (FSI: So long, Glad to meet you, thanks, Good evening, I'm very sorry). | Verified against the FSI OCR text and the Wiktionary responses. Kept the cards (the usual modern English equivalents, and short stock phrases that are not protectable) and corrected the record: method step on phrases, fsi.usedFor, wiktionary.usedFor and the licensing paragraph now say the English is the authors' choice of the usual equivalent, name FSI's wording, and say that it is the same as Wiktionary's gloss. | fixed |
| — | The record never said where the Swedish of the phrases, por favor and abuelo/abuela came from; it is the same as the Folkets entries looked up, while the record said nothing was taken from Folkets. | Verified in the Folkets XML. The method's card-writing step, folkets.usedFor and the licensing paragraph now say that where no CC0 source gives Swedish, the Swedish is the standard equivalent and the same as the Folkets entry it was checked against, that these are single words or fixed greetings (facts of usage, not protectable expression) and that no definitions, examples or selection were used. CC0 stands. | fixed |
| all cards with RAE evidence | The report quotes about 130 all-rights-reserved RAE definitions, some long, with no notice separating them from the deck's CC0 and the repository's MIT licence. | Every RAE quotation longer than 90 characters is cut to the headword, the grammatical label and the first words of the sense, ending in "…" (de nada keeps only sense 2; the apocope note of uno is kept whole, as it is the fact the note relies on). The licensing paragraph now says that quotations in the report are not covered by the deck's CC0 or the repository's MIT licence and names the rights in each source's quotations. | fixed |
| querer, ver | The only content-source evidence is a Wikidata lexeme without senses; the meaning rests on verification sources, and the querer note copied Wiktionary's "to be fond of". | Verified in the FSI OCR text: Unit 1 p. 1.3 "(I) want (to want)" — "quiero (querer)"; Unit 6 p. 6.1 "let's see (to see)" — "veamos (ver)" and the vocabulary appendix "(ver) … to see 6.1". Added these as evidence. The querer note is reworded: "Also “to love” someone or something." (RAE querer 2). | fixed |
| — | The method said the scripts and raw responses are kept, but they were only in a temporary scratch directory, and the look-up code for RAE, Folkets and Wiktionary was not recorded. | The cross-checking step now says the raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published; the RAE text extraction, the Wiktionary parsing and the Folkets index and matching code are recorded verbatim in queries 12–14, and the review-round look-ups in queries 15–18. | fixed |
